item.content:encoded:
Current HDR Students

发布源: 9. Center for Water Economics, Environment and Policy, Crawford School, Australian NationalUniversity  – Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-07

CWEEP convenes public interest research on water economics and policy in Australia & the Asia-Pacific

The Centre for Water Economics, Environment and Policy (CWEEP – pronounced ‘sweep’) is a focal point for applied research, dialogues, policy and public engagement, and other work that contributes to improving the health and well-being of waterways and the human societies that dependent upon them.

Established in 2010 by Professor Quentin Grafton, CWEEP has convened policy-research dialogues, led applied research, and supported water education to strengthen water governance and environmental sustainability. Our research associates are leading researchers and practitioners whose expertise spans economics, institutional design, hydrology, geography, and beyond. Since 2024, CWEEP's work has been led by Dr Paul Wyrwoll with a focus on four core areas: dam reoperation, waterway restoration, the human right to water, and innovations in water pricing, markets and finance.

CWEEP’s research on water economics and policy is founded upon a systems perspective of trade-offs, decisions, and interactions. The scope of our work explicitly extends beyond understanding freshwater systems: we seek to inform and enable actions that address unsustainable water use, water injustice, and climate change. We value and support community-led research, deliberation, and advocacy that seeks to effect policy reform.

item.title: [Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia] Social Services Reforms
item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
Social Services Reforms

发布源: Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-07

In their current form, Australia’s social services are failing too many people.

Inaccessible, inconsistent, and unaffordable services are compounding inequality. Narrow eligibility criteria force people to navigate complex services or wait until they are in crisis.

From early childhood development to employment services, CPD works to change the way we deliver social services so that they truly work to support the community.

We envision a government that is more connected to communities, more hands-on, and that provides universally accessible, but not uniform, services that meet individuals’ needs.

Putting People Firstis a report that lays out a bold vision to transform social services to genuinely meet the needs of the people and communities they are designed to support.

It identifies six key drivers for reform and four practical steps governments can take now to create a system people can trust and depend on.

Growing Togetheris a report from the Centre for Policy Development’s early childhood development initiative, building on our landmarkStarting Betterreport andGuarantee for children and families.

It outlines essential steps for achieving a truly universal early education and care system.

Starting Betteris a landmark report from the Centre for Policy Development that proposes a guarantee for young children and families – a new pillar of Australia’s social deal.

Delivering the guarantee will make Australia the best place to be a child, and raise a family.

item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
Wellbeing Government in Australia

发布源: Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-07

Improving the wellbeing of current and future generations requires a shift in mindset when it comes to what we think ofas progress.

We promote policy approaches that meet the needs of people and the environment, that are values-driven, holistic and preventative.

Seeing policy ideas through a wellbeing lens leads to decisions that reflect community values, respect environmental bounds and deploy resources more effectively for the common good.

Our vision is to embed wellbeing at the heart of Australian policymaking in a way that will lead to effective and systemic change.

Avoidable Costsis a report that addresses the substantial costs governments incur by failing to address the root causes of issues, and makes the financial case for prevention and tackling problems early.

Embedding Progressis a report from the Centre for Policy Development that provides governments with a practical manual for how to achieve better outcomes for the people they serve.

TheWellbeing Economy in Briefseries is a collection of mini briefing papers that look at the idea of a wellbeing economy, how it relates to other ideas for economic change, and what some of the core elements of a wellbeing economy are.

item.content:encoded:
‘Bleak City’ is set to become marvellous again

发布源: Grattan Institute --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-07

by Aruna Sathanapally

Another day, another bleak assessment of the state of Victoria, and its capital, Melbourne.

Since the pandemic, it has been hard to avoid them. Even walking around the city centre has been a reminder of vibrancy lost. For the city hardest hit by the pandemic, the road back is a long one.

This is clearest in the state’s finances. All budgets (save Western Australia’s) are under pressure. But Victoria has gone from a relatively rich state to a relatively poor state, ahead of only Tasmania and South Australia. And with healthcare spending on the rise, infrastructure investment still at record levels, and the threat of a difficult bushfire season ahead, budget pressuresaren’t likely to ease any time soon.

But that is not the full story of Melbourne’s fortunes: the city could be on the cusp of an economic renewal.

Melbourne has long held a strong position in the battle of Australian cities when it comes to quality of life. It has consistently ranked as Australia’s most liveable city, and during much of the 2010s as the most liveable in the world. This year it was votedTime Out’s best city worldwide. Culture, sports, food, trams, and green spaces have made Melbourne marvellous.

But right now, the real ace Melbourne has up its sleeve is its housing market.

item.content:encoded:
Budget reboot: How to fund Australia’s future

发布源: Grattan Institute --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-07

by Aruna Sathanapally, Erin-Lea Brown, Matthew Bowes, Ashleigh Chang

Australia needs a budget reboot. Over the past decade, government spending has outgrown revenue. Low interest rates have kept the cost of borrowing down, even as debt grew.

Download the report

Download the chart data

Download the technical supplement

But since the COVID pandemic, the game has changed. Cost-of-living pressures, rising demand for social services, and higher borrowing costs have sent state debt skyward, and pushed the federal budget back into deficit.

And those pressures will build over the decades ahead. An ageing population will drive health and care spending even higher. More frequent and severe natural disasters will present a mounting bill for all governments. Federal governments will face demands to give back bracket creep, even as the income tax base shrinks. And high interest rates may well weigh on the budget for years to come.

The problem is most acute in state budgets, where the surpluses to reduce debt are increasingly out of reach. States are struggling with spending growth, particularly for health. They are failing to bank revenue windfalls, and their fiscal targets are too vague to bind.

State taxes – including stamp duty and mining royalties – are more volatile than those raised by the federal government, and won’t keep pace with future needs. While ‘tied’ grants from the federal government are increasingly filling this gap, the federal budget faces many of the same pressures.

item.content:encoded:
How to fund Australia’s future

发布源: Grattan Institute --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-07

by Erin-Lea Brown, Matthew Bowes

Australia’s budgets are under pressure. Debt is rising, interest bills are climbing, and the costs of an ageing population and climate change are still ahead. So how did we get here? And what would it take to fix it?

The biggest challenges now sit in state budgets, and the GST is no longer doing the job it was designed to do.

In this podcast, Grattan Economic Prosperity Deputy Program Director Erin-Lea Brown talks to Senior Associate Matthew Bowes about our report,Budget reboot: How to fund Australia’s future, which sets out a plan to repair budgets through stronger fiscal rules, a bigger and broader GST, and a new deal between federal and state governments.

Erin-Lea Brown:Budget pressure is rising across Australia’s federation. Both the federal government and the state governments are staring down escalating debt, and rising interest rates will add billions more to the bill. We are moving into a harder and more expensive world, and the demands on state and federal governments keep increasing.

This matters because of the known risks ahead. From an ageing population and the growing costs of climate change, to rising demand for health and disability services, all of these pressures will require governments to have the fiscal firepower to act.

So how did Australia get here, and what would it take to fix it?

That’s the focus of Grattan’s new report,Budget reboot: How to fund Australia’s future.
